'''Richard Neece Ojeda II''' ({{IPAc-en|oʊ|ˈ|dʒ|ɛ|d|ə}} {{Respell|oh|JED|ə}}; born October 25, 1970) is an American politician and retired [[United States Army]] [[Major (United States)|major]] who is the member-elect for [[North Carolina's 9th congressional district]]. A member of the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]], he previously served in the [[West Virginia Senate]], representing the [[West Virginia's 7th Senate district|7th district]] from January 2017 until January 2019, and ran a brief campaign for [[President of the United States]] in [[2020 United States presidential election|the 2020 election]].

Raised in [[Logan, West Virginia]], Ojeda graduated from [[West Virginia State University]] and [[Webster University]]. He initially joined the [[United States Army]] as an [[enlisted rank|enlisted soldier]] and [[Mustang (military officer)|went through officer training after finishing college]]. During his 25 years in the military, Ojeda earned two [[Bronze Star Medal]]s and rose to the rank of major. He served two tours of duty in Iraq and spent over fifteen years during his service at [[Fort Bragg]] near [[Fayetteville, North Carolina]]. After retiring, he initially worked as a [[Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps]] teacher before running for office.

Ojeda was elected to the West Virginia Senate in [[2016 West Virginia Senate election|2016]]. He received national attention during his [[2018 United States House of Representatives elections in West Virginia|2018 campaign]] for the United States House of Representatives for [[West Virginia's 3rd congressional district]], when he became a vocal supporter of [[2018 West Virginia teachers' strike|the 2018 teachers' strike]] and advocated for the legalization of [[cannabis in West Virginia]]. He would ultimately be defeated in that election. 

In November 2018, Ojeda announced his candidacy for president in the 2020 election, but he dropped out in January 2019 when his campaign failed to gain traction. In January 2020, Ojeda announced he would instead challenge [[incumbent]] [[United States Senate|U.S. Senator]] [[Shelley Moore Capito]] in the [[2020 United States Senate election in West Virginia|2020 election]], but he failed to secure the Democratic nomination in the primary. 

Following his 2020 campaigns, Ojeda moved back to [[North Carolina]], and won the Democratic primary for [[North Carolina's 9th congressional district]] in the [[2026 United States House of Representatives elections in North Carolina#District 9|2026 election]] in March 2026. Ojeda defeated incumbent [[Richard Hudson (American politician)|Richard Hudson]], the chair of the [[National Republican Congressional Committee]], on November 3, 2026. 

==Early life and education==
Ojeda was born in [[Rochester, Minnesota]], the son of Florena (Pansera) and Richard N. Ojeda.<ref>{{Cite web |title=FamilySearch |website=[[FamilySearch]]|url=https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VC8Q-CHS}}</ref> He was born into a Democratic family and he registered as a Democrat. He remarked that "back when I was in high school, being a Republican was like cursing". Ojeda's paternal grandfather, Senon H. Ojeda, was an immigrant from the [[Mexican Americans|Mexican]] state of [[Jalisco]] who came to West Virginia during the coal boom to try to make a living, and later gained citizenship. One of Ojeda's grandparents died in a mining accident after fighting in World War II. Ojeda's father was born in the United States, but moved to Mexico and lived there until the age of eight. Ojeda's father worked as a nurse anaesthetist.<ref name="politico" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=[[Larissa MacFarquhar]] |date=November 10, 2016 |title=Learning Trump Won, in West Virginia |url=https://www.newyorker.com/news/news-desk/learning-trump-won-in-west-virginia |access-date=April 14, 2018 |newspaper=[[The New Yorker]]}}</ref><ref name="heart">{{Cite web |last=MacFarquhar, Larissa |date=October 10, 2016 |title=In the Heart of Trump Country |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2016/10/10/in-the-heart-of-trump-country |access-date=April 14, 2018 |newspaper=[[The New Yorker]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Schwartzmann, Gabe |date=March 15, 2018 |title=Analysis: The Mountain State's Labor Tradition |url=http://www.dailyyonder.com/analysis-mountain-states-labor-tradition/2018/03/15/24361/ |access-date=April 14, 2018 |newspaper=The Daily Yonder}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=The Young Turks |title=Richard Ojeda's Presidential Bid Gains Steam! |date=November 24, 2018 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bpGGITdMl3M |access-date=January 21, 2019}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=Grim |first=Ryan |date=November 12, 2018 |title=Richard Ojeda, West Virginia Lawmaker Who Backed Teachers Strikes, Will Run for President |url=https://theintercept.com/2018/11/11/richard-ojeda-2020-president/ |access-date=May 31, 2021 |website=[[The Intercept]] |language=en-US}}</ref> Ojeda also has Italian ancestry.<ref>{{Cite web |last=II |first=Richard N. Ojeda |date=January 8, 2019 |title=My grandfathers came to America from Mexico and from Italy for opportunity. When immigrants STOP wanting to come to this country, that is when we will have a real crisis. #TrumpAddress #BoycottTrump #weareworthy |url=https://twitter.com/VoteOjeda2020/status/1082751220501151746}}</ref>

Ojeda graduated from [[Logan High School (West Virginia)|Logan High School]] in 1988.<ref name=heart/><ref name="politico" /> He earned a bachelor's degree in General Education from [[West Virginia State University]] and a master's degree in Business and Organizational Security from [[Webster University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ojeda's education |url=https://votesmart.org/candidate/biography/147777/richard-ojeda-ii#.WgEhH0yZPVo}}</ref>

==Military service and teaching career==
[[File:MAJ Richard Ojeda (cropped).jpg|upright|thumb|Army portrait (2013)]]
Ojeda said "Where I come from, when you graduate high school, there’s only three choices—dig coal, sell dope, or join the Army. And I chose the military". He served 25 years in the [[United States Army]], starting as an enlisted soldier before going through officer training and rising to the rank of major.<ref name="politico" /> His first orders sent him to serve in [[North Carolina]] at [[Fort Bragg]] in 1997, where he would spend the majority of his military career.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |last=Lopez |first=Robert |date=2026-02-26 |title=Richard Ojeda Takes on MAGA in Deep Red North Carolina |url=https://barnraisingmedia.com/richard-ojeda-takes-on-maga-in-deep-red-north-carolina/ |access-date=2026-04-29 |website=Barn Raiser |language=en-US}}</ref> In 2004, he assumed command of a company in the [[20th Engineer Brigade (United States)|20th Engineer Brigade]] and immediately deployed with them to [[Iraq]] as part of the [[Iraq War]].<ref name="politico" /><ref>{{Cite web |last= |date=2020-06-04 |title=VoteVets PAC Endorses Richard Ojeda for US Senate |url=https://votevets.org/press-releases/votevets-pac-endorses-richard-ojeda-for-us-senate |access-date=2026-04-29 |website=VoteVets |language=en-US}}</ref> He earned two Bronze Stars.<ref name="politico" /> During his service, he also spent time in South Korea, Honduras, Jordan, Haiti, Afghanistan.<ref name="politico" /> When not deployed abroad, Ojeda spent over 15 years based back at Fort Bragg, the post he was first ordered to upon entering the Army, when not deployed abroad.<ref name=":7" />

[[File:2BCT Partners With Haitian Government to Restore Transportation Routes in Port-au-Prince DVIDS245356.jpg|thumb|upright|Ojeda (left) in [[Haiti]] in 2010, assisting with relief efforts after the [[2010 Haiti earthquake|2010 earthquake]]]]
After retiring from the military, Ojeda worked as a [[Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps|Junior ROTC]] instructor at [[Chapmanville Regional High School]] from 2013 to 2017, resigning due to time constraints related to his service as state senator, in addition with his run for Congress.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news  |first=Rusty |last=Marks |title=Senator warns of possible teacher strike |language=en |work=WV News |url=https://www.wvnews.com/news/wvnews/senator-warns-of-possible-teacher-strike/article_74ad118b-8cb3-5837-9624-d08a02f1937b.html |access-date=May 9, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Takitch |first=Nathan |date=2017-05-29 |title=W.Va. State Senator resigns from Logan County JROTC program |url=https://www.wsaz.com/content/news/WVa-State-Senator-resigns-from-Logan-County-JROTC-program-425147134.html |access-date=2026-09-10 |website=WSAZ3 |language=en}}</ref> He helped start a [[Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps]] at a local high school. He established a social services nonprofit, the Logan Empowerment Action and Development, which engaged in community cleanup, Christmas toy drives, providing meals for the needy, and raising money for shoes for kids. During this time, Ojeda also started penning letters to the editor of the ''Logan Banner''. As a result, Ojeda was invited by Senator [[Joe Manchin]] of West Virginia to the 2013 State of the Union address as a guest. Ojeda decided to enter politics while listening to Manchin discuss disparities in allocation of "manufacturing hubs" to different regions of West Virginia.<ref name="politico" />

==Political career==
Ojeda entered politics in 2014, running for Congress in West Virginia's 3rd District. He garnered 34% of the vote in the Democratic primary, losing to incumbent [[Nick Rahall]], whom Ojeda challenged on the grounds that the incumbent was not doing enough to advance the interests of the district.<ref name="Kruse">{{Cite web |last=Kruse |first=Michael |title='You're Going to Know My Name! I'm Richard Ojeda!' |url=https://politi.co/2ARpzwM |access-date=January 21, 2019 |website=[[Politico]] |date=November 7, 2018 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="politi.co">{{Cite web |last=Kruse |first=Michael |title='He's JFK With Tattoos and a Bench Press' |url=http://politi.co/2HWbtMp |access-date=January 21, 2019 |website=[[Politico]] |date=March 2, 2018 |language=en}}</ref>

===West Virginia Senate===
Ojeda was assaulted at a primary campaign event on May 8, 2016, in [[Logan County, West Virginia]]. The assailant, Jonathan S. Porter, who had ties to Ojeda's opponent, received 1–5 years in prison, and a $500 fine as a part of a plea deal.<ref name="politi.co" /><ref name="Stelloh 2016">{{Cite web |last=Stelloh |first=Tim |date=May 9, 2016 |title=West Virginia State Senate Candidate, a Veteran, Brutally Beaten |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/west-virginia-state-senate-candidate-veteran-brutally-beaten-n570271 |access-date=June 4, 2017 |website=[[NBC News]]}}</ref><ref name="WSAZ">{{Cite web |last=Staff |first=WSAZ News |title=UPDATE: Man sentenced for beating of state senator |url=https://www.wsaz.com/content/news/West-Virginia-State-Senate-candidate-injured-in-attack-378578156.html |access-date=January 22, 2019 |website=www.wsaz.com |date=May 8, 2016 |language=english}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Hauser |first=Christine |date=2016-05-09 |title=Attack on West Virginia State Senate Candidate Overshadows Vote |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/10/us/attack-on-state-senate-candidate-overshadows-west-virginia-vote.html |access-date=2026-04-29 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Ojeda went on to win the Democratic primary for the 7th District of the [[West Virginia Senate]], defeating incumbent [[Art Kirkendoll]].<ref name="WSAZ" /> In the general election, held on November 8, 2016, he defeated Republican Jordan Bridges by almost 18 points.<ref>{{Cite news |date=August 1, 2017 |title=West Virginia 7th District State Senate Results: Richard Ojeda Wins |language=en-US |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/elections/2016/results/west-virginia-state-senate-district-7 |access-date=January 25, 2019 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

In the West Virginia Senate, Ojeda sponsored the West Virginia Medical Cannabis Act, legislation to legalize medical marijuana, which was signed into law by Governor [[Jim Justice]] on April 19, 2017.<ref name="Barren 2017">{{Cite web |last=Barren |first=Amanda |date=April 19, 2017 |title=UPDATE: Gov. Justice signs medical marijuana bill into law |url=http://www.wsaz.com/content/news/WVa-Senate-approves-medical-marijuana-bill-417527793.html |access-date=June 4, 2017 |website=WSAZ}}</ref><ref name="politico" /> In the Senate, he called for increases in teacher wages, arguing that low pay would lead to strikes and teachers leaving the state.<ref name=":0" /> In January 2018, he criticized West Virginia Governor [[Jim Justice]]'s proposed 1–2% increase in teacher wages, saying it was insufficient.<ref name=":0" />

Ojeda has stated "I don't think I've ever voted for a Democrat for president" and supported [[Donald Trump]] in 2016.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ball |first=Krystal |date=January 12, 2016 |title=This could be the future of the Democratic Party |url=https://www.facebook.com/vicenews/videos/951157501710867/ |access-date=January 13, 2018 |website=[[Vice (magazine)|Vice]] |publisher=HBO}}</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20181112215556/https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/can-a-trump-voter-from-west-virginia-win-the-2020-democratic-primary/ Can A Trump Voter From West Virginia Win The 2020 Democratic Primary?]. [[FiveThirtyEight]]. November 12, 2018.</ref> He told ''[[Politico]]'' that he voted for Trump because he initially believed Trump would do something for West Virginians. By 2018, he expressed regret for voting for Trump, saying that "he hasn't done shit" and he is "taking care of the daggone people he's supposed to be getting rid of".<ref name="politico">{{Cite news |last=Kruse |first=Michael |date=March 2, 2018 |title='He's JFK With Tattoos and a Bench Press' |publisher=[[Politico]] |url=https://www.politico.com/magazine/story/2018/03/02/richard-ojeda-west-virginia-blue-army-one-217217/}}</ref> Ojeda said he supported [[Bernie Sanders]] in the [[Democratic Party presidential primaries, 2016|2016 Democratic primary]].<ref name="mj">{{Cite web |last=Murphy, Tim |date=May 8, 2018 |title=He Voted for Trump. Now He's Running for Congress as a Pro-Pot, Pro-Coal Democrat. |url=https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2018/05/he-voted-for-trump-now-hes-running-for-congress-as-a-pro-pot-pro-coal-democrat |access-date=May 8, 2018 |newspaper=[[Mother Jones (magazine)|Mother Jones]]}}</ref>

Ojeda resigned from the West Virginia Senate on January 14, 2019, citing frustration with the legislature's slow pace and his inability to accomplish all his legislative goals.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McElhinny |first=Brad |date=January 15, 2019 |title=Ojeda submits official Senate resignation letter, citing frustration |url=http://wvmetronews.com/2019/01/15/ojeda-submits-official-senate-resignation-letter-citing-frustration/ |access-date=January 16, 2019 |website=[[West Virginia MetroNews]]}}</ref>

==== Teacher strikes ====
Ojeda rose to prominence for his early support of and leading role in the [[2018 West Virginia teachers' strike]].<ref name=":5" /> A month before the strike, Ojeda, in a speech on the Senate floor, called on his fellow legislators to heed the complaints and requests of teachers lest a strike be inevitable.<ref name="politi.co" /> He then introduced several bills, including ones addressing public employees' healthcare needs, raising their wages, and giving teachers tax deductions on purchased classroom supplies.<ref name="Campbell">{{Cite web |last=Campbell |first=Alexia Fernández |date=May 8, 2018 |title=Richard Ojeda's West Virginia primary win gives Democrats their best chance to turn coal country blue |url=https://www.vox.com/2018/5/8/17332674/ojeda-west-virginia-primary-2018 |access-date=January 21, 2019 |website=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]}}</ref> Due to his active and vocal support of the strikes, Ojeda was said by some to have attained something of a "folk hero" status with teachers and other unionists. He was regularly met by chants of his last name and other expressions of appreciation and commendation while traveling the state to speak out in support of the strikers (and later his Congressional bid).<ref name="politi.co" /><ref name="Kruse" /><ref name="Campbell" />

Ojeda traveled to [[California]] to support the 2019 [[Los Angeles]] teachers' strike, proclaiming "Don’t make us go West Virginia on you" in an [[op-ed]] published in ''[[The Intercept]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ojeda |first=Richard |date=January 16, 2019 |title=Richard Ojeda on the LA Teachers Strike: "Don't Make Us Go West Virginia on You" |url=https://theintercept.com/2019/01/16/la-teachers-strike-richard-ojeda/ |access-date=January 21, 2019 |website=[[The Intercept]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

===2018 U.S. House campaign in West Virginia===
{{main|2018 United States House of Representatives elections in West Virginia#District 3}}

Ojeda ran for [[West Virginia's 3rd congressional district]], a seat which was vacated by Republican [[Evan Jenkins (politician)|Evan Jenkins]], who filed instead to run in the primary for the [[U.S. Senate]].<ref name="Charleston Gazette-Mail 2017">{{Cite web |last=Ferguson |first=F. Brian |date=May 11, 2017 |title=Ojeda, Phillips latest to declare runs for Congress |url=http://www.wvgazettemail.com/news-politics/20170511/ojeda-phillips-latest-to-declare-runs-for-congress |access-date=June 4, 2017 |website=Charleston Gazette-Mail}}</ref><ref name="GrigoryanSuetzl178191">{{Cite book |last1=Grigoryan |first1=Nune |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=D_CYDwAAQBAJ |title=Alternative Media Meets Mainstream Politics: Activist Nation Rising |last2=Suetzl |first2=Wolfgang |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |year=2019 |isbn=9781498584357 |editor-last=Atkinson |editor-first=Joshua D. |pages=178, 191 |chapter=Hybridized political participation |editor-last2=Kenix |editor-first2=Linda}}</ref> His campaign was staffed in part by local residents who were working on the campaign without pay, and held private jobs while working on the campaign.<ref name="politico" /> According to Ojeda, the only donations he accepted were from individual donors and labor unions. He won the Democratic primary on May 9, 2018, defeating [[Shirley Love (politician)|Shirley Love]], Janice Hagerman, and Paul Davis.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fernández Campbell, Alexia |date=May 9, 2018 |title=Richard Ojeda's West Virginia primary win gives Democrats their best chance to turn coal country blue |url=https://www.vox.com/2018/5/8/17332674/ojeda-west-virginia-primary-2018 |access-date=May 9, 2018 |publisher=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]}}</ref>

''[[Salon.com|Salon]]'' noted that Ojeda's race was a potential [[Bellwether (politics)|bellwether]], noting that "Ojeda is no stranger to converting Trump supporters: He won his state Senate election by 18 points, in a district Trump carried by 59."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Derysh |first=Igor |date=2018-10-13 |title=Could Democrats flip a West Virginia district Trump won by 49 points? |url=https://www.salon.com/2018/10/13/could-democrats-flip-a-west-virginia-district-trump-won-by-49-points/?utm_source=website&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=ogshare&utm_content=og |access-date=2026-04-29 |website=Salon.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

During the campaign, Ojeda agreed to an interview for Michael Moore's documentary, ''[[Fahrenheit 11/9]]''. Ojeda's off the cuff unpolished pronouncements were used by opponent [[Carol Miller (politician)|Carol Miller]]'s campaign to bring under question Ojeda's patriotism while labeling him as unhinged.<ref name="Kruse" /> Ojeda took issue with Miller's criticism in a campaign ad.<ref>{{Citation |last=Richard Ojeda |title=COUNTRY |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ofh_QHho_qA |access-date=January 21, 2019}}</ref>

As the polling began to indicate a tight race, President Trump traveled to West Virginia in October to campaign for Miller. On the stump, Trump mocked Ojeda while making a point of pronouncing Ojeda's last name while affecting an Hispanic accent.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bonn |first=Tess |date=November 9, 2018 |title=Ojeda hits back at Trump: I will gladly be your 'stone cold crazy wacko' |url=https://thehill.com/hilltv/rising/415936-ojeda-hits-back-at-trump-i-will-gladly-be-your-stone-cold-crazy-wacko |access-date=January 21, 2019 |website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Kruse" />

On November 6, 2018, Ojeda was defeated in the general election by 12 points, winning 44% of the vote to Miller's 56%. For Democrats, this was a 32-point improvement in performance from the previous election, where the Democrat won only 24% to the Republican's 68%.<ref>{{Cite web |title=WV SOS - Elections - Election Results - Online Data Services |url=http://services.sos.wv.gov/apps/elections/results/results.aspx?year=2016&eid=23&county=Statewide |website=services.sos.wv.gov |access-date=November 21, 2017 |archive-date=December 25, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161225112543/http://services.sos.wv.gov/apps/elections/results/results.aspx?year=2016&eid=23&county=Statewide |url-status=dead }}</ref> According to ''[[FiveThirtyEight]],'' Ojeda outperformed his district's partisan lean by 25%, the strongest showing for a non-incumbent.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rakich |first=Nathaniel |date=2018-11-20 |title=Everything Is Partisan And Correlated And Boring |url=https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/everything-is-partisan-and-correlated-and-boring/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181120212131/https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/everything-is-partisan-and-correlated-and-boring/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=November 20, 2018 |access-date=2019-11-08 |website=[[FiveThirtyEight]]|language=en-US}}</ref>

In November 2018, Ojeda filed with the [[Federal Election Commission]], officially becoming [[2020 United States presidential election|a candidate for President of the United States]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 12, 2018 |title=W.Va. Sen. Richard Ojeda officially announces run for president in 2020 |url=https://www.wsaz.com/content/news/State-Senator-Richard-Ojeda-to-run-for-President-in-2020-500248782.html |access-date=November 12, 2018 |website=WSAZ}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=January 26, 2019 |title=RICHARD OJEDA DROPS OUT OF PRESIDENTIAL RACE |url=https://theintercept.com/2019/01/25/richard-ojeda-president-drops-out/ |access-date=January 26, 2019 |website=[[The Intercept]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Hall |first=Steven |title=Form 1 for Ojeda for President |url=http://docquery.fec.gov/cgi-bin/forms/C00691444/1291151/ |access-date=November 11, 2018 |publisher=[[Federal Election Commission]] |language=en-US}}{{Usgovpd}}</ref><ref name="WSAZ breaking news">{{Cite web |last=WSAZ News Staff |date=November 11, 2018 |title=State Senator Richard Ojeda to run for President in 2020 |url=https://www.wsaz.com/content/news/State-Senator-Richard-Ojeda-to-run-for-President-in-2020-500248782.html |access-date=November 12, 2018 |website=wsaz.com |language=en-US}}</ref> His campaign was announced on November 11, at a Louisville, Kentucky, rally which consisted mostly of union members.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Raymond |first=Adam K. |date=2018-11-20 |title=Richard Ojeda Isn't Like Other Democrats. Is That a Good Thing? |url=https://nymag.com/intelligencer/2018/11/richard-ojeda-isn%27t-like-other-democrats-is-that-good.html |access-date=2019-09-06 |website=[[New York (magazine)|New York Intelligencer]] |language=en }}{{Dead link|date=September 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> His campaign focuses included ending government corruption and returning the Democratic Party to a party that benefited the working class.<ref name=":5" /> As no incumbent state legislator has ever mounted a serious bid for the presidency, Ojeda was considered a "longshot" and "underdog" candidate.<ref>{{Citation |title=BREAKING: Richard Ojeda Running For President In 2020 | date=November 12, 2018 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dlTfjcJ77ls |language=en |access-date=2019-09-06}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Malone |first=Clare |date=2018-11-12 |title=Can A Trump Voter From West Virginia Win The 2020 Democratic Primary? |url=https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/can-a-trump-voter-from-west-virginia-win-the-2020-democratic-primary/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181112215556/https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/can-a-trump-voter-from-west-virginia-win-the-2020-democratic-primary/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=November 12, 2018 |access-date=2019-09-06 |website=[[FiveThirtyEight]]|language=en-US}}</ref>

He resigned from the West Virginia Senate on January 9, 2019, to focus on his presidential bid.<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 15, 2019 |title=Ojeda submits official Senate resignation letter, citing frustration |url=http://wvmetronews.com/2019/01/15/ojeda-submits-official-senate-resignation-letter-citing-frustration/ |access-date=January 29, 2019 |website=WV MetroNews |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web  |first=Jake|last= Zuckerman |title=After resigning from WV Senate, Ojeda ends presidential bid |url=https://www.wvgazettemail.com/news/politics/after-resigning-from-wv-senate-ojeda-ends-presidential-bid/article_94625b45-6125-54f1-a8e4-47ff085f570a.html |access-date=January 29, 2019 |website=Charleston Gazette-Mail |date= January 25, 2019 |language=en}}</ref> A few days after, Ojeda asked the Senate Minority Leader (a Democrat) if he could rescind his resignation, with the Senate Minority Leader telling Ojeda to talk to the Senate President (a Republican) because that is the person to whom he sent the resignation letter.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Banner |first=Dylan Vidovich Logan |title=Justice picks lobbyist to fill Ojeda's term in Senate |url=https://www.wvgazettemail.com/news/legislative_session/justice-picks-lobbyist-to-fill-ojeda-s-term-in-senate/article_2b604c31-f9fb-533f-8599-2538d7c41e19.html |access-date=January 29, 2019 |website=Charleston Gazette-Mail |date=January 17, 2019 |language=en}}</ref> The Republican governor, [[Jim Justice]], seated lobbyist [[Paul Hardesty]] in Ojeda's vacant seat.<ref name=":1" /> Ojeda dropped out of the race on January 26, 2019.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Grim |first=Ryan |author-link=Ryan Grim |date=2019-01-25 |title=Richard Ojeda Drops Out of Presidential Race |url=https://theintercept.com/2019/01/25/richard-ojeda-president-drops-out/ |access-date=2025-11-17 |website=The Intercept |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Merica |first=Dan |date=2019-01-25 |title=Richard Ojeda ends short-lived 2020 campaign {{!}} CNN Politics |url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/01/25/politics/ojeda-ends-2020-campaign |access-date=2025-11-17 |website=CNN |language=en}}</ref>

====Endorsements====
{{main|Endorsements in the 2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries#Richard Ojeda}}

===2020 U.S. Senate campaign in West Virginia===
{{Further|2020 United States Senate election in West Virginia}}

On January 13, 2020, Ojeda announced his campaign for the [[United States Senate]], hoping to challenge incumbent [[Shelley Moore Capito]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Budryk |first=Zack |date=2020-01-13 |title=Democrat Richard Ojeda announces Senate bid after dropping out of presidential race |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/478011-democrat-richard-ojeda-announces-senate-bid-after-dropping-out-of |access-date=2020-01-14 |website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Pierson |first=Lacie |date=2020-01-13 |title=Familiar names surge during first day of filing for 2020 election in West Virginia |url=https://www.wvgazettemail.com/news/politics/familiar-names-surge-during-first-day-of-filing-for-election/article_c8bc2230-1da8-515a-8c2f-46d8c0608e6e.html |access-date=2020-01-14 |website=Charleston Gazette-Mail |language=en}}</ref> On June 9, 2020, Ojeda was defeated in the [[2020 United States Senate election in West Virginia|primary election]] by five points, winning 33% of the vote, as opposed to [[Paula Jean Swearengin]]'s 38%.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-06-10 |title=West Virginia State Primary Election Unofficial Results |url=https://results.enr.clarityelections.com/WV/103231/web.247524/#/detail/25 |access-date=2020-06-10 |website=Clarity Elections: Election Night Reporting |publisher=West Virginia Secretary of State}}</ref> Following the primary, Ojeda endorsed Swearengin for the general election.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Thomas |first=Alex |date=2020-07-10 |title=Swearengin receives Sanders endorsement |url=https://wvmetronews.com/2020/07/09/swearengin-receives-sanders-endorsement/ |access-date=2025-11-17 |website=WV MetroNews |language=en-US}}</ref>

===2026 U.S. House Campaign in North Carolina===
{{Further|2026 United States House of Representatives elections in North Carolina#District 9}}

Ojeda moved back to [[North Carolina]] in 2020, where he had previously lived for over fifteen years during his military career.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Solender |first=Andrew |date=2025-10-15 |title=Scoop: Democrat Richard Ojeda raises $1.2M in bid to oust House GOP campaign chair |url=https://www.axios.com/2025/10/15/richard-hudson-ojeda-fundraising-north-carolina |access-date=2025-11-17 |website=Axios |language=en}}</ref> Ojeda announced a campaign for [[North Carolina's 9th congressional district]] in the [[United States House of Representatives]] in 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Simms |first=Austin |date=April 1, 2025 |title=Former West Virginia state senator Richard Ojeda announces congressional bid in North Carolina |url=https://www.lootpress.com/former-west-virginia-state-senator-richard-ojeda-announces-congressional-bid-in-north-carolina/ |access-date=2025-11-17 |website=Lootpress |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Early |first1=Steve |last2=Gordon |first2=Suzanne |date=2025-11-14 |title=The Left-Leaning Military Veterans Eyeing Congress |url=https://jacobin.com/2025/11/military-veterans-progressive-candidates-congress |access-date=2025-11-17 |website=Jacobin |language=en-US}}</ref> By October 2025, Ojeda raised $1.2 million from 20,000 donors with an average contribution of $16 each, in his bid to oust [[National Republican Congressional Committee]] Chair [[Richard Hudson (American politician)|Richard Hudson]].<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last=Early |first=Steve |last2=Gordon |first2=Suzanne |date=2025-11-14 |title=The Left-Leaning Military Veterans Eyeing Congress |url=https://jacobin.com/2025/11/military-veterans-progressive-candidates-congress |access-date=2026-04-29 |website=Jacobin |language=en-US}}</ref>

On March 3, 2026, he won the Democratic nomination for the district.<ref>{{Cite web |last=AP |date=2026-03-03 |title=Richard Ojeda wins Democratic nomination for U.S. House in North Carolina's 9th Congressional District |url=https://www.caledonianrecord.com/news/national/richard-ojeda-wins-democratic-nomination-for-u-s-house-in-north-carolinas-9th-congressional-district/article_616494ce-ed8b-5d33-ad0f-dd2e0d444482.html |access-date=2026-03-04 |website=Caledonian Record |language=en}}</ref> His win was praised by the North Carolina [[AFL-CIO]], which cited his work as a "very strong advocate for unions" in a race roundup article.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |date=2026-03-06 |title=Labor 2026 Update on NC Primary Election Results {{!}} North Carolina State AFL-CIO |url=https://aflcionc.org/news/labor-2026-update-nc-primary-election-results |access-date=2026-04-29 |website=NC AFL-CIO |language=en}}</ref> After his victory, he was a keynote speaker at a [[Fayetteville, North Carolina|Fayetteville]] [[No Kings protests|No Kings rally]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hutson |first=Beth |title=A No Kings rally is set for Fayetteville. What to know if you're going |url=https://www.fayobserver.com/story/news/local/2026/03/24/fayetteville-nc-no-kings-rally-scheduled-for-march-28-protest-trump-administration-policies/89283979007/ |access-date=2026-04-29 |website=The Fayetteville Observer |language=en-US}}</ref> 

Ojeda narrowly beat Richard Hudson in the [[2026 United States elections|November 3 election]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Woolverton |first=Paul |date=2026-11-04 |title=Meet Richard Ojeda, the Vet Who Beat ‘Fort Bragg’s Congressman’ Richard Hudson |url=https://www.cityviewnc.com/stories/richard-ojeda-defeats-richard-hudson-us-house/ |access-date=2026-11-05 |website=CityView NC |language=en-US}}</ref> 

==Political positions==
===Ideological orientation===
Ojeda has been described by some as a [[Populism|populist]] of the "[[Left-wing politics|left-wing]] [[Left-wing populism|variety]]".<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Murphy, Tim |date=May 9, 2018 |title=West Virginia's Surging Democrat Richard Ojeda Slams Trump |url=https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2018/05/richard-ojeda-slams-trump |newspaper=[[Mother Jones (magazine)|Mother Jones]]}}</ref><ref name="Heins">{{Cite web |last=Heins |first=Scott |date=2018-03-07 |title=As West Virginia Strike Winds Down, Angry Teachers Look to Bolster Progressives in Elections |url=https://theintercept.com/2018/03/07/west-virginia-teacher-strike-midterm-elections/ |access-date=2019-01-21 |website=[[The Intercept]] |language=en-US}}</ref> He identifies as a traditional working-class Democrat and laments what he perceives as a Democratic party that is increasingly drifting away from its working-class roots and becoming a party of the elite.<ref name=":5" /> In the [[2016 Democratic Party presidential primaries|2016 Democratic presidential primary]], he says he voted for [[Independent politician|Independent]] Senator [[Bernie Sanders]].<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Garofoli |first1=Joe |date=2019-01-04 |title=With a West Virginia drawl, Democrat gives working class a voice in 2020 |url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/With-a-West-Virginia-drawl-Democrat-gives-13507167.php |access-date=2020-01-19 |website=SFChronicle.com |language=en-US}}</ref> He has also been described as a [[New Democrats (United States)|moderate Democrat]] and he stated that he voted for President Donald Trump in the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 presidential election]] (a decision he later regretted).<ref>{{Cite news |last=Gerety |first=Rowan Moore |date=2018-10-05 |title=Richard Ojeda's Politics of Regret |journal=The Nation |language=en-US |url=https://www.thenation.com/article/richard-ojedas-politics-of-regret/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181005132344/https://www.thenation.com/article/richard-ojedas-politics-of-regret/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=October 5, 2018 |access-date=2020-01-19 |issn=0027-8378 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Pathé |first1=Simone |date=2020-01-13 |title=West Virginia's Richard Ojeda is back, this time running for Senate |language=en |url=https://www.rollcall.com/news/campaigns/west-virginias-richard-ojeda-back-time-running-senate |access-date=2020-01-19 |archive-date=January 15, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200115025027/https://www.rollcall.com/news/campaigns/west-virginias-richard-ojeda-back-time-running-senate |url-status=dead }}</ref> He describes himself as a "conservative on most cultural issues" who supports coal jobs and border security.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hunt |first=Albert R. |title=How to be a Democrat in blue-collar Trump country |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/opinion/commentary/ct-perspec-democrat-trump-country-richard-ojeda-west-virginia-0918-story.html |access-date=2020-01-19 |website=chicagotribune.com|date=September 17, 2018 }}</ref>

=== Taxes ===
Ojeda was one of the few West Virginia lawmakers who came out outspokenly in favor of raising taxes on corporations and the rich, calling for higher corporate taxes (particularly on coal and gas corporations that were the major economic players in WV) to offset spending cuts that had negatively affected public services and employees in the state.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=Campbell |first=Alexia Fernández |date=2018-05-08 |title=Richard Ojeda's West Virginia primary win gives Democrats their best chance to turn coal country blue |url=https://www.vox.com/2018/5/8/17332674/ojeda-west-virginia-primary-2018 |access-date=2019-01-21 |website=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]}}</ref>

=== Labor rights ===
Ojeda is devoutly pro-union and received $121,440 during his 2018 campaign from several unions, including the [[American Federation of Teachers]] and the [[Teamsters' Union]].<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite tweet |number=1078431503980343296 |user=VoteOjeda2020 |title=What does real economic growth look like? It looks like 30 million new union jobs where we not only unionize green jobs to implement the GND but we also professionalize and unionize community workers including healthcare, child care, prevention and more. |date=December 27, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Richard Ojeda II's Campaign Finances - The Voter's Self Defence System |url=https://votesmart.org/candidate/campaign-finance/147777/richard-ojeda-ii#.XD9uBFxKi1s |access-date=2019-01-16 |website=Vote Smart |language=en}}</ref> In his 2026 North Carolina campaign, Ojeda received an endorsement from the NC [[AFL-CIO]].<ref name=":8" /> Ojeda opposes [[right-to-work law]]s.<ref name=":3" />

=== Veterans affairs ===
Ojeda, a veteran himself, has advocated for improved services for those who have served in the military, arguing that the United States has a fundamental obligation to care for veterans following their service.<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |last=Serrano |first=Patricia |date=2026-02-27 |title=Richard Ojeda II is running to represent District 9 in the United States House of Representatives |url=https://enlacelatinonc.org/en/Richard-Ojeda-II-aspires-to-represent-District-9-in-the-United-States-House-of-Representatives/ |access-date=2026-04-29 |website=Enlace Latino NC |language=en}}</ref> He supports expanding [[United States Department of Veterans Affairs|Veterans Affairs]] (VA) benefits, particularly around [[mental health care]].<ref name=":10" /> His 2026 [[North Carolina]] congressional campaign collected 90,000 signatures for a petition that criticized the [[Trump administration]] cuts to VA services as part of the larger [[Department of Government Efficiency]] (DOGE) cuts.<ref name=":9" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Lopez |first=Robert |date=2026-02-26 |title=Richard Ojeda Takes on MAGA in Deep Red North Carolina |url=https://barnraisingmedia.com/richard-ojeda-takes-on-maga-in-deep-red-north-carolina/ |access-date=2026-04-29 |website=Barn Raiser |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Gun control===
On [[gun control]], Ojeda has early in his political career been described as pro-gun.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fernandez Campbell |first=Alexia |date=2018-11-12 |title=Democrat Richard Ojeda, a champion of West Virginia's teachers, says he is running for president |url=https://www.vox.com/policy-and-politics/2018/11/12/18087534/richard-ojeda-runs-for-president-west-virginia |access-date=2019-12-22 |publisher=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]}}</ref> In 2018, he stated that increased services for the mentally ill would help ease gun violence. At the time, he noted that he supported the Second Amendment and does not believe additional restrictions are needed.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Delancey |first=Sean |date=2018-11-04 |title=Miller and Ojeda: Where they stand on gun control |url=https://wchstv.com/news/local/miller-and-ojeda-where-they-stand-on-gun-control |access-date=2019-12-22 |publisher=WCHS}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Out favorite pro-gun Democrats |url=http://www.theprogundemocrat.com/favorite-pro-gun-democrats-richard-ojeda-west-virginia.html |access-date=2019-12-22 |publisher=The Pro-gun Democrat}}</ref>

However, on August 8, 2019, following the [[2019 Dayton shooting|Dayton]] and [[2019 El Paso shooting|El Paso]] shootings, Ojeda shifted his position and called pro-gun rights politicians "spineless pieces of shit" who "didn't have the balls" to take on the NRA.<ref name="NowThis" /> He also called for stricter gun restrictions, citing a series of recent mass shootings that had collectively accounted for a total of 74 deaths.<ref name="NowThis">{{cite news |title=Retired Army Major Makes Passionate Plea for Gun Reform |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D082LCOpPU8|date=August 8, 2019|work=Now This}}</ref>

===Foreign policy===
Ojeda, on his [[Twitter]] account has posted several tweets opposed to [[Saudi Arabia]] and the [[Saudi Arabian-led intervention in Yemen|intervention]] it leads in support of the [[Yemeni government]] against the Iranian-backed [[Houthi]]s that had [[Houthi takeover in Yemen|taken]] over much of Yemen's north including its capital, [[Sanaa]]. He stated that the US should end support for Saudi Arabia and end arms deals with the nation; he also condemned the country for the alleged involvement of the Saudi government in [[Jamal Khashoggi]]'s death.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-12-04 |title=Ojeda on Saudia Arabia |url=https://twitter.com/VoteOjeda2020/status/1070063527476514816 |access-date=2019-12-22 |publisher=[[Twitter]]}}</ref>

Regarding [[Iran]], Ojeda has stated he would not support a war with Iran.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-05-14 |title=Ojeda on Iran |url=https://twitter.com/VoteOjeda2020/status/1128440581703782400 |access-date=2019-12-22 |publisher=[[Twitter]]}}</ref>

===Abortion===
Ojeda self-identifies as pro choice. He supports [[abortion]] rights and that he would nominate only those judges who share his support for access to abortion.<ref name="Grim">{{Cite web |last=Grim |first=Ryan |date=2018-11-21 |title=Richard Ojeda Comes Out Swinging on Abortion Rights |url=https://theintercept.com/2018/11/21/richard-ojeda-abortion-president/ |access-date=2020-01-19 |website=[[The Intercept]] |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web  |first=Matt|last=Combs  |title=Ojeda discusses his platform in Hinton |url=https://www.register-herald.com/news/ojeda-discusses-his-platform-in-hinton/article_5d42c1af-50e9-5d11-9e34-f5c80b0c02f5.html |access-date=2020-01-19 |website=Beckley Register-Herald |date=March 28, 2018 |language=en}}</ref> He said that he hates "the idea of telling a woman what to do with her body" and noted that he supported ''[[Roe v. Wade]]'' and [[Planned Parenthood]] in an interview with ''The Guardian'' in 2018.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lartey |first=Jamiles |date=2018-02-27 |title=Could this 'military guy' Democrat find a magic formula to win back blue-collar voters? |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2018/feb/27/could-this-military-guy-democrat-find-a-magic-formula-to-win-back-blue-collar-voters |access-date=2026-04-29 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> He has also voiced opposition to the [[Helms Amendment to the Foreign Assistance Act|Helms Amendment]] that limits the United States in assistance to abortion through foreign aid, saying, "a woman raped by the [[Taliban]] or [[Boko Haram]] should not be forced by the callousness of our government to bear her rapist’s child".<ref name="Grim" />

=== Healthcare ===
During his 2026 North Carolina congressional campaign, Ojeda noted his support for expanding Medicaid and protecting the Affordable Care Act.<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |last=Battaglia |first=Danielle |date=February 25, 2026 |title=Four NC Democrats want to take longtime Rep. Richard Hudson’s seat in Congress |url=https://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/election/article314548430.html |access-date=April 29, 2026 |website=The News & Observer}}</ref> Ojeda in 2018 stated that Congress and the president should be barred from taking out extra insurance, and should instead have to rely on the standard healthcare which would be afforded every American citizen for the course of their terms of office, to incentivize them in promoting and maintaining quality comprehensive universal healthcare coverage.<ref name=":4">{{Citation |last=The Young Turks |title=Richard Ojeda's Presidential Bid Gains Steam! |date=November 24, 2018 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bpGGITdMl3M |access-date=2019-01-21}}</ref>

=== Environment ===
Ojeda has called for sustainable energy.<ref name="Heins" /> Ojeda has noted that he sees a limited role for coal in steel-making for the foreseeable future but has acknowledged that coal is "not gonna come back", and expressed his desire to find a way for miners to transition into other well-paying jobs.<ref name=":5" /> During his 2018 congressional campaign, Ojeda praised the Trump administration's plan to roll back environmental regulations and stated it would benefit the coal industry and bring back jobs to his district.<ref name=":5" />

=== Immigration ===
In a 2016 interview with ''The New Yorker'' during the presidential election that year, Ojeda said he understood the frustrations of working-class communities that made them receptive to Donald Trump's messaging on restricting benefits for undocumented immigrants.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=MacFarquhar |first=Larissa |date=2016-10-03 |title=In the heart of Trump country |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2016/10/10/in-the-heart-of-trump-country |access-date=2019-12-22 |magazine=The New Yorker}}</ref> As Trump's administration began enacting immigration policy changes, Ojeda shifted leftward in response.<ref name="Heins" /> He has since spoken out against the Trump administration's policy of separating migrant children from their parents at the border.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bonn |first=Tess |date=June 19, 2018 |title=West Virginia Dem who backed Trump sickened by family separations |url=https://thehill.com/hilltv/rising/392994-west-virginia-sen-richard-ojeda-takes-issue-with-president-trumps-zero/ |access-date=April 29, 2026 |website=The Hill}}</ref> In his 2026 congressional campaign, Ojeda has identified changing federal immigration policy as his top priority, and has been critical of [[United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement|Immigration and Customs Enforcement]] (ICE) raids.<ref name=":11" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Serrano |first=Patricia |date=2026-02-27 |title=Richard Ojeda II is running to represent District 9 in the United States House of Representatives |url=https://enlacelatinonc.org/en/Richard-Ojeda-II-aspires-to-represent-District-9-in-the-United-States-House-of-Representatives/ |access-date=2026-04-29 |website=Enlace Latino NC |language=en}}</ref> Ojeda supports [[Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals]] and a pathway to citizenship for "Dreamers".<ref name=":4" /><ref name="Heins" />

=== Cannabis ===
Ojeda has called for the [[Decriminalization of non-medical cannabis in the United States|legalization of marijuana]] and clemency for those incarcerated for possession.<ref name=":2">{{Cite tweet |number=1078429643609378816 |user=VoteOjeda2020 |title=What does real criminal justice reform and attacking the opioid epidemic look like? It starts with no longer arresting people for simple possession and instead referring them to treatment. It looks like legalizing cannabis and letting people in our jails on those charges...out. |date=December 27, 2018}}</ref> During his tenure as state senator, Ojeda spearheaded the passage of a bill legalizing medical marijuana.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kruse |first=Michael |title=He's JFK With Tattoos and a Bench Press |url=http://politi.co/2HWbtMp |access-date=2019-01-21 |website=[[Politico]] |date=March 2, 2018 |language=en}}</ref> He advocates directing funds raised from taxes on cannabis sales to fund public works.<ref name="Heins" />

=== Pharmaceutical companies ===
Ojeda has taken stances against the [[pharmaceutical industry]], focusing in particular on its role in sparking the [[opioid epidemic]].<ref name=":5" /> During his 2018 campaign, Ojeda noted that he would not take money from drug companies and would "throw their lobbyists out of my office."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Facher |first=Lev |date=2018-10-19 |title=Eight midterm races putting pharma — and its influence — front and center |url=https://www.statnews.com/2018/10/19/midterms-pharma-drug-prices/ |access-date=2026-04-29 |website=STAT |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Campaign finance, political ethics, and transparency ===
As described by Ojeda, his presidential campaign focused on "lobbying and corruption in Washington", and proposed measures to address political ethics.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":0" /> Ojeda proposed requiring body-cams on lobbyists in order to increase government transparency and public oversight.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |date=December 22, 2018 |title=Richard Ojeda: Let's make lobbyists wear body cameras |url=https://ky.aflcio.org/news/richard-ojeda-lets-make-lobbyists-wear-body-cameras |access-date=December 31, 2018 |website=Kentucky State AFL-CIO |language=en |archive-date=January 1, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190101051522/https://ky.aflcio.org/news/richard-ojeda-lets-make-lobbyists-wear-body-cameras |url-status=dead }}</ref> He is a supporter of [[Wolf PAC|WolfPAC]], and has pledged not to take corporate donations for his campaign.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":6" />

Ojeda has proposed that to prevent exploitation of political office for personal financial gain, federally elected officials and Cabinet officials must donate to charity any net worth exceeding one million dollars. He proposed that, upon retirement from public office, such officials must be subject to an annual earnings limit of $120,000 (in addition to a $130,000 pension), "subject to automatic yearly cost of living adjustments."<ref name="Mission">{{Cite web |title=Mission |url=https://voteojeda.com/mission/ |access-date=December 31, 2018 |website=Richard Ojeda for President 2020 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":5" /> Ojeda also called for implementing "donor vouchers," allocated funds that would give individual voters small amounts of money to donate to the candidate of their choice, to enhance the financial sway of individual, poorer voters.<ref>{{Cite tweet |number=1078432798820786176 |user=VoteOjeda2020 |title=Each voter gets a donor voucher for a small amount that they can give to their candidate of their choice.https://twitter.com/camillekimball/status/1078430882933788672 … |date=December 27, 2018}}</ref>
